- If sentiment is consistently low or negative (≤0.5) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; adjust forecast downward by 1–3%.
- If model shows steady upward drift (e.g., +0.1–0.3 per day) without sentiment support, it overreacts to recent highs; cap growth rate or introduce mean reversion.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast slope by 20–40% for next 3–5 days.
- When true outcome shows early sharp decline (e.g., 3–5 days of falling prices), model often lags; shift forecast downward by 1–2 days with 0.5–1.0% per day adjustment.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.8) and model is flat or rising slowly, it underestimates volatility; add 0.5–1.5% upward bias for next 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome by >5% for 3+ consecutive days, apply downward correction with exponential decay (e.g., 10% reduction per day until convergence).
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.7) and model is trending, check for horizon mismatch — 30-day forecasts often overfit recent trends; use 15-day smoothing or sentiment-weighted average.
